parts.problem_md:
In what ways is Lennie significant in Of Mice and Men?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

As one of the novel’s protagonists, Lennie is a deeply significant character in Of Mice and Men and his character reveals key themes such as vulnerability, dreams, power and isolation. Through Lennie, Steinbeck illustrates the harshness of 1930s America and critiques how society treats those who are different.

Lennie is first introduced as a physically powerful character but is vulnerable because of his learning difficulties. Steinbeck uses contrasting imagery to highlight the differences between Lennie and George. While George has “sharp”, “strong” and “slender” features, Lennie is described as “shapeless of face” with “large, pale eyes” which immediately sets him apart. Steinbeck also uses animalistic language to describe Lennie. For instance, it states that he was “dragging his feet a little, the way a bear drags his paws” and that he “bleated with terror”. These comparisons emphasise both Lennie’s physicality and his innocence. His strength, combined with his lack of understanding, makes him both dangerous and deeply vulnerable.

Lennie’s childlike innocence is evident through his love of soft things such as mice, puppies and rabbits, and he even dreams of tending rabbits on the farm he and George hope to own. His repeated desire to “live off the fatta the lan’” is symbolic of the American Dream and his childlike enthusiasm helps keep the dream alive for both him and George. Lennie’s firm belief in the dream offers hope and companionship in a world which is defined by loneliness and economic hardship. This dream becomes even more poignant when considering the context of the Great Depression, a time when many itinerant workers like George and Lennie were left hopeless and rootless.

Lennie is significant because his actions foreshadow later events in the novel. Early in the novel, Lennie, not realising his own strength, inadvertently kills a mouse by petting it too hard. Later, he accidentally kills a puppy given to him by Slim, exclaiming, “I didn’t bounce you hard”. Finally, and most tragically, he kills Curley’s wife in the barn when she allows him to stroke her hair. These events reveal how Lennie’s inability to control his strength leads inevitably to catastrophe. His actions reinforce Steinbeck’s theme of inevitable failure and how even the purest dreams cannot survive in a world governed by brutality and misunderstanding.

Lennie is also depicted as a victim and Curley views Lennie as an easy target for his hatred. Candy explains that Curley “hates big guys” which suggests that Lennie’s physical presence threatens insecure men. During Curley’s attack in the bunkhouse, Lennie only retaliates under George’s command, crushing Curley’s hand in a moment that is both defensive and destructive. Lennie fails to understand the consequences of his strength and this misunderstanding makes him a danger to others and himself. Yet Steinbeck does not portray Lennie as malicious. Instead he ensures readers see Lennie as a tragic figure shaped by a world that has no real place for him.

The novel also shows how society deals with people like Lennie. When he runs away after killing Curley’s wife, he hides in the brush, remembering George’s instructions. A lynch mob forms and although George briefly considers Lennie might be locked up, Slim reminds him that Lennie would not survive such treatment. The threat of institutionalisation, of being put in a “booby hatch”, reflects the limited social care available for those with learning difficulties during the 1930s. Therefore Lennie’s fate is a commentary on the cruelty of a system that punishes rather than protects the vulnerable.

Lennie’s death is one of the most significant moments in the novel. George shoots Lennie as an act of mercy, protecting him from the mob. Lennie dies while imagining the dream, with George describing the farm to him one last time and this allows Lennie to die peacefully, believing the dream is within reach. Steinbeck uses this ending to suggest that Lennie, ironically, comes closest to realising the dream as he dies believing it will actually happen. This reinforces the tragedy that in 1930s America, dreams like theirs were often doomed by poverty and social prejudice.

In conclusion, Lennie is a deeply significant character in Of Mice and Men. He embodies the themes of innocence, vulnerability and broken dreams. Through Lennie, Steinbeck explores how society marginalises the weak and how, in a world full of violence and inequality, even the most hopeful dreams are often crushed. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This response demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of Lennie’s significance and engages closely with both textual detail and contextual insight. The candidate explores Lennie’s role structurally, thematically and symbolically, offering nuanced interpretations of his innocence, strength and vulnerability. The essay shows a clear, developed argument and remains focused on the question throughout. Context is effectively woven into the discussion of itinerant life during the Great Depression, attitudes towards learning disabilities and the harsh realities of American society in the 1930s. The commentary on Lennie’s animalistic description and the moral complexity of his death reflect strong critical thinking. Quotations are well-chosen and effectively integrated. Overall, this is a mature, balanced and insightful response. > **[exam-tip]** > - Show how **Lennie’s strength and innocence** make him both powerful and vulnerable > - Track how Lennie’s **accidental violence escalates**, foreshadowing tragedy > - Explore how **Lennie keeps the dream alive** — even if he can’t survive to see it > - Use **context** on the **Great Depression** and treatment of people with **disabilities** > - Reflect on how **Lennie is treated by others**, especially Curley, George and Crooks > - Explain how **Lennie’s death** is both an act of **mercy** and a **comment on society**

parts.problem_md:
Discuss the importance of settings in the novel.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In Of Mice and Men, Steinbeck uses setting not only to establish atmosphere but also to reflect the themes of isolation, vulnerability and broken dreams. From the peaceful clearing by the pool to the stark bunkhouse and Crooks’ room, each location in the novel helps to shape the reader’s understanding of the characters’ lives and the harsh realities they face.

The novel begins and ends at the natural clearing by the pool, an idyllic space that Steinbeck describes through rich imagery. The water is still, the trees are leafy and the animals scurry around peacefully. This scene evokes the Garden of Eden and it is juxtaposed with the grim world of the ranch. During the Great Depression, millions of itinerant workers travelled with little more than bedrolls, often camping outdoors like George and Lennie. The “smooth” branch near the pool shows that many others have sat in the same spot and are part of an endless cycle of poverty. However, Steinbeck also uses this same setting as a place of death at the end of the novel and when Lennie returns there, nature reflects the tension and violence which is about to occur. For instance, Steinbeck describes how the heron swallows the water snake, symbolising the survival of the fittest. Here, Steinbeck uses the natural world to show both the beauty and brutality of life.

The bunkhouse is another key setting, reflecting the bleakness of itinerant workers’ lives. Steinbeck describes it as a “long, rectangular building” with whitewashed walls, lacking warmth or comfort. There are no personal possessions, just bunks and a “black cast-iron stove”. The bunkhouse is depicted as a place of masculinity and hierarchy, where Curley asserts dominance and where Lennie is vulnerable. The claustrophobic nature of this space contrasts with the openness of the outdoors, symbolising how the characters are trapped in repetitive, hopeless routines. This reflects the Great Depression, when millions of men like George and Lennie travelled for work but found no security.

The barn is equally important as a setting. It is initially portrayed as a place of warmth and Slim gives Lennie one of Lulu’s pups there. However, this becomes the setting for two major deaths: the puppy and Curley’s wife. When Lennie kills the puppy, Steinbeck uses this to foreshadow the later tragedy of Curley’s wife. The horses sense unease as they stamp their feet and “rattle” their “halter chains”. The barn thus becomes a place of danger and death, reinforcing Steinbeck’s idea that dreams, like Lennie’s desire to tend rabbits, are destined to fail in such a brutal world. It also highlights the fragility of life for people like Lennie and Curley’s wife, who, as someone with learning disabilities and a woman respectively, are both powerless and misunderstood.

Crooks’ room is another symbolic setting. It is a “little shed” off the barn, filled with broken equipment and harnesses, showing both his role as a stable buck and his position in the social hierarchy of the ranch. Crooks sleeps on a “long box filled with straw”, which is worse than the white ranch hands’ basic bunks, revealing how black people were segregated and dehumanised. Steinbeck uses this setting to reflect Crooks’ isolation: he is both physically and socially excluded. Crooks tells Lennie, “A guy needs somebody — to be near him,” reinforcing the novel’s theme of loneliness. His room, like his life, is separated from the rest and is another reflection of racial prejudice in 1930s America.

Time also plays a crucial role in the novel’s setting. The story takes place over just a few days, adding urgency and a sense of inevitability. Events move quickly: the men arrive on Friday, spend Saturday in town and by Sunday afternoon, Curley’s wife is dead. This compressed timeline mirrors the fragile nature of the characters’ dreams and highlights how quickly hope can turn to despair. Further, the novel’s setting in Soledad, meaning solitude, also reinforces the theme of loneliness which is depicted in each setting.

In conclusion, Steinbeck uses settings not simply to describe where things happen, but to deepen the reader’s understanding of the characters and their world. The contrast between the natural world and man-made spaces reflects the loss of freedom, while settings like Crooks’ room and the barn show how racism, loneliness and crushed dreams define life on the ranch. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a mature and well-structured response that closely examines how Steinbeck’s settings contribute to meaning. The candidate integrates contextual knowledge seamlessly, particularly regarding the Great Depression, racial segregation and the symbolic nature of locations like Soledad. There is a clear focus on how settings reveal character experiences and reinforce key themes such as isolation, vulnerability and the fragility of dreams. Each paragraph explores a different setting and links it back to the novel’s wider concerns. The use of quotations is selective and well integrated and the candidate demonstrates a consistent awareness of how atmosphere, symbolism and historical context contribute to Steinbeck’s message. The exploration of the novel’s framing with the clearing by the pool is particularly effective. This is a confident and insightful response. > **[exam-tip]** > - Focus on **how each setting reveals character emotions** and experiences > - Contrast the **natural world** with man-made spaces like the **bunkhouse** and the **barn** > - Use **context** — especially the **Great Depression** and **social segregation** > - Don’t forget how **time settings** add urgency and deepen the novel’s atmosphere > - Explain how settings like **Crooks’ room** symbolise **social exclusion** > - Show how **Steinbeck uses atmosphere** to build tension or reflect loss

parts.problem_md:
Discuss the theme of responsibility in Of Mice and Men

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

Steinbeck explores the theme of responsibility in Of Mice and Men through the characters’ relationships, the moral choices they make and the wider social context of 1930s America. The theme is particularly evident in how characters respond to the needs of others and the consequences of their actions.

The clearest example of personal responsibility is seen in George’s relationship with Lennie. From the start, George is presented as a reluctant guardian, having promised Lennie’s Aunt Clara that he would look after him. This sense of duty drives George’s every decision. The novel is set during the Great Depression, when economic hardship meant people had to fend for themselves. Most men travelled alone, focused only on survival. George and Lennie’s companionship stands in contrast to this reality, offering a glimpse of a more compassionate way of living that the world around them ultimately rejects. Although he occasionally expresses frustration, "God a'mighty, if I was alone I could live so easy", his actions consistently reveal deep care. Furthermore, Lennie’s mental disability and the lack of support systems reflect the social attitudes of the time. Institutions for the mentally ill and those with learning disabilities were often brutal, and George’s actions can be seen as protecting Lennie from a cruel system. George’s protective behaviour, like instructing Lennie not to talk to the boss, reflects the weight of this responsibility. Steinbeck contrasts George’s loyalty with the usual loneliness of itinerant workers, highlighting the unusual and burdensome nature of this relationship.

Responsibility is also explored in George’s final decision to shoot Lennie. This act is both shocking and compassionate. Rather than allow Lennie to fall into the hands of Curley’s lynch mob, George takes responsibility for ending his life peacefully. By doing so, George spares Lennie from a brutal death and prevents future tragedies. Steinbeck presents this as a heavy moral burden, one that isolates George completely by the end. The choice reflects a deeper, more painful form of responsibility: taking accountability even when there are no good options.

Slim, the "prince of the ranch" is another character who embodies responsible behaviour. He is respected and trusted and his calm authority means others look to him for moral guidance. When Candy’s old dog is to be shot, Slim is the one whose opinion is most valued: “Candy looked a long time at Slim to try to find some reversal”. Slim’s quiet leadership contrasts with Carlson’s blunt insensitivity and his giving of the puppy to Lennie unintentionally sets up the novel’s climax, demonstrating how even responsible acts can have unintended consequences.

Similarly, Candy’s relationship with his old dog is an example of evading moral responsibility. Although he clearly cares for the animal, Candy allows Carlson to take on the task of euthanising it, rather than doing it himself. He later confesses bitterly, “I ought to of shot that dog myself”, a statement that not only reveals his guilt but also foreshadows George’s decision to shoot Lennie personally. Later in the novel, Candy is quick to invest in George and Lennie’s dream, offering his life savings in exchange for security. His eager declaration, “S'pose I went in with you guys. Tha's three hunderd an' fifty bucks I'd put in” suggests he sees the dream as a way to avoid taking charge of his future in a world that has discarded him due to age and disability.

Steinbeck also uses characters who shirk responsibility to explore the theme from another angle, showing how inaction or selfishness can be just as destructive as misguided duty. Curley’s wife, though often portrayed as a victim of loneliness and gender inequality, also demonstrates a lack of awareness, or disregard, for the consequences of her behaviour. She repeatedly seeks out Lennie, despite knowing his unpredictable nature. When she says, “Why can't I talk to you? I never get to talk to nobody” it reflects her need for attention but also her manipulation of a dangerous situation. Her decision to let Lennie stroke her hair directly contributes to the tragic climax. Steinbeck shows how irresponsible actions, even when driven by desperation or isolation, can have fatal outcomes.

In conclusion, Steinbeck uses multiple characters and situations to show how responsibility can be a burden, a moral duty and a force for good or harm. Through George, Slim, Candy and others, he suggests that in an unforgiving world, taking responsibility for others is both noble and tragic. Ultimately, Steinbeck critiques a society that fails to support the vulnerable, leaving responsibility in the hands of individuals who are often unequipped to bear it alone. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This response would be placed in the top band of the mark scheme. It remains sharply focused on the question throughout, offering a clearly developed and informed personal response. Interpretations of characters and events are insightful and the essay demonstrates close knowledge of the text. Context is seamlessly integrated to support the argument, especially in relation to the historical setting and social structures of 1930s America. Evidence is well-selected and consistently supports the points made and the essay shows an excellent balance between analysis and interpretation. > **[exam-tip]** > - Track how characters like **Candy**, **Slim** and **Curley’s wife** respond to **responsibility** — or avoid it > - Explore how Steinbeck links **responsibility** to **isolation**, **mercy** and **survival** in a **harsh world** > - Use **context** on the **Great Depression** and **lack of care** for **people with disabilities** in 1930s America > - Reflect on how characters are held **accountable** for their actions — even when **intentions are good** > - Explain how **George’s final act** is both **compassionate** and a **critique** of a **broken society**

parts.problem_md:
Explore Candy’s relationship with others, including his old dog, in the novel.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In Of Mice and Men, Steinbeck presents Candy as a deeply isolated character whose relationships with others reveal the harsh realities of ageing, disability and loneliness during the Great Depression. Candy’s connections, to his dog, to George and Lennie and to the wider group of men, are shaped by his fear of being discarded, but also by his longing for companionship and purpose.

Candy’s most emotionally significant relationship is with his old dog, which acts as a reflection of his own vulnerability. The dog, described as a “dragfooted sheepdog, gray of muzzle, and with pale, blind old eyes” symbolises Candy’s own fate on the ranch: once useful though now seen as worthless. Candy’s reluctance to have the dog put down, even when others argue it is the kindest thing, shows how deeply attached he is. Carlson’s insistence that the dog “ain’t no good to himself” reflects the brutal mindset of the ranch, where people and animals are valued only for their ability to work. Candy’s eventual agreement, and his haunting regret “I ought to of shot that dog myself”, reveal his internal conflict. It also foreshadows George’s decision to take responsibility for Lennie’s death, highlighting the novel’s theme of mercy and duty.

Candy’s relationship with George and Lennie is one of hope and dependency. When Candy overhears them discussing their dream of owning land, he is quick to offer his life savings to be part of it. His excitement is palpable: “S’pose I went in with you guys... I won’t have no place to go, an’ I can’t get no more jobs.” Steinbeck uses this relationship to explore how people on the margins of society — the old, the disabled, the outcast — yearn for connection. Candy’s desperation drives him to cling to this dream, not just for economic security but for emotional belonging. Candy’s position on the ranch is unusual because, unlike most itinerant workers, he has savings which was a rare advantage during the Great Depression. After losing his hand in a ranch accident, Candy received compensation and has since been given an undemanding job. However, Steinbeck shows that even this security is fragile. At the time, there was no meaningful state support for the elderly or disabled and Candy knows his usefulness is limited. Candy sees in George and Lennie a rare opportunity for stability, purpose and dignity and his willingness to contribute financially also shows his deep need to be needed.

However, this bond is ultimately fragile. When Lennie kills Curley’s wife and the dream dies, Candy is devastated. His bitter outburst, “You God damn tramp... Ever'body knowed you'd mess things up”, reveals not just his grief but his powerlessness. Candy lashes out at Curley’s wife, not because he truly blames her alone, but because her death represents the end of his only chance at belonging. This reaction exposes the harsh emotional cost of being denied companionship and the cruel reality of broken dreams.

Candy’s interactions with the other men on the ranch are marked by a sense of inferiority. His age and missing hand set him apart and he often remains on the sidelines. He acts as a source of information for George and Lennie when they arrive, telling them about the characters and the rules of the ranch, but his role is largely passive. He is not respected in the way Slim is, nor is he feared like Curley. When conflict arises, Candy has little influence, and he relies on others to protect or include him. This reflects the broader context of 1930s America, where older workers were easily replaced and left with no support.

Candy’s treatment of Crooks also reveals the limits of his empathy. When Crooks suggests he could join in on the dream too, Candy initially allows it. But when Curley’s wife threatens Crooks, Candy quickly backs down, unwilling to challenge the racial hierarchy. This moment exposes the conditional nature of Candy’s friendship as he is not willing to risk his own fragile place to defend someone more vulnerable. Steinbeck uses this moment to show how even the oppressed can be complicit in maintaining social divisions.

Throughout the novel, Candy’s relationships reflect Steinbeck’s exploration of loneliness, usefulness and the human need for companionship. His bond with his dog is a symbol of his own fate and his hope in George and Lennie’s dream highlights his desire for connection. Yet, Candy is ultimately powerless, excluded by a society that values youth and strength over loyalty and humanity. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a convincing and well-structured response that meets the criteria for the highest band of the mark scheme. The argument remains sharply focused on the question, exploring how Candy’s relationships reflect broader social issues of isolation, usefulness and companionship. The essay uses precise textual references to support thoughtful points, and integrates short, well-selected quotations to deepen analysis. Context is also handled with skill and references to the Great Depression, disability and economic vulnerability are integrated seamlessly into the discussion of Candy’s experiences, enhancing understanding without dominating the argument. > **[exam-tip]** > - Track how Candy’s **relationships** reflect his fear of **isolation**, especially after **losing his hand** > - Explore how his **old dog** acts as a **symbol** for Candy himself — **ageing**, **disabled**, and **unwanted** > - Analyse how his **attachment** to George and Lennie’s **dream** reveals his deep **need for belonging and purpose** > - Use the **context** of the **Great Depression** and the **lack of support** for the **elderly and disabled** to explain his anxiety > - Explain how Steinbeck uses Candy to **criticise a society** that only values people when they are **physically useful**

parts.problem_md:
‘Several characters have little or no power at all.’

How far do you agree with this view?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

Powerlessness is a central theme in Of Mice and Men and Steinbeck presents a world in which several characters are unable to control their own lives. These characters are defined not only by their lack of physical or social power, but also by the wider historical context of the Great Depression, which left many people vulnerable and voiceless. Through figures like Lennie, Crooks, Candy and Curley’s wife, Steinbeck shows how individuals are denied power by disability, race, gender and circumstance.

Lennie is one of the most obviously powerless characters. Although physically strong, his mental disability means that he is unable to understand or control his actions. This leads to him accidentally killing his puppy and, later, Curley’s wife. Steinbeck shows that Lennie is entirely dependent on George, who tells him what to eat, where to go and what to say. When the boss becomes suspicious, George must explain, “He’s dumb as hell, but he ain’t crazy”. Lennie himself says, “I tried not to forget. Honest to God I did, George” showing how little power he has over his own mind. The wider context of the 1930s also adds to Lennie’s lack of power. The Great Depression, high unemployment and the collapse of financial institutions meant that men became itinerant farm workers, forced to travel constantly in search of work. Workers like Lennie and George were at the mercy of bosses who could fire them at any time. There was no provision for those with disabilities, and attitudes towards race and gender further entrenched inequality. Ultimately, Lennie is so powerless that George must take the decision to kill him, believing it the only way to save him from a worse fate.

Candy is another character whose lack of physical strength leaves him without power. After losing his hand in an accident, he is unable to work alongside the other men and is given the job as a swamper. Despite being offered compensation, Candy remains deeply insecure about his position on the ranch. He is unable to stop Carlson from shooting his old dog, and later regrets not taking responsibility himself: “I ought to of shot that dog myself”. His relationship with the dog symbolises his own vulnerability — both of them are old, disabled, and seen as no longer useful. Candy’s excitement at George and Lennie’s dream of owning land reflects his desperation to escape a future where he will be left with nowhere to go.

Curley’s wife is similarly presented as a powerless character, isolated and ignored on account of her gender. As the only woman on the ranch, she is referred to by her husband’s name rather than her own. The men see her as “jail bait” and a “rattrap” and she is often left alone. She reveals her past to Lennie, telling him she could have been in the “pitchers”. Her decision to marry Curley was not based on love, but on escaping a life with no other options. Even in her final moments, she is powerless. Lennie silences her as she screams and she dies without anyone knowing what truly happened. Her death silences her permanently, reinforcing her lack of agency.

Crooks is another character who is denied power by both racism and segregation. He lives alone, apart from the other men and Steinbeck describes him as having “reduced himself to nothing”. When Curley’s wife threatens him by saying, “I could get you strung up on a tree so easy it ain’t even funny”, Crooks retreats entirely, realising how little protection or justice he can rely on. The harsh treatment he receives is typical of 1930s America. At the time, the Ku Klux Klan was prevalent and lynching was commonplace. Despite a moment of connection when he speaks to Lennie and Candy about the dream, Crooks pulls away, saying, “Nobody never gets to heaven, and nobody gets no land”. His hopelessness reveals how racism has stripped him of any sense of possibility or self-worth.

Even George, who appears to have more control than most, is ultimately shown to be powerless in the face of violence and injustice. When Curley decides to hunt Lennie down, George is left with no choice but to act before Curley does. He kills Lennie himself in a moment that is both merciful and deeply tragic, highlighting the futility of their dream and the impossibility of escape.

In conclusion, Steinbeck presents a world in which several characters have little or no power at all. Their fates are shaped not just by individual weakness but by a society that marginalises the vulnerable. Through their stories, Steinbeck critiques a system that devalues humanity in favour of strength, status and survival. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a well-developed and thoughtful response that would be placed securely in the top band of the mark scheme. The argument is clearly focused on the theme of powerlessness, using a wide range of characters to support this claim. The candidate demonstrates an informed personal response and a critical style is maintained throughout, particularly in the treatment of Lennie, Candy, Curley’s wife and Crooks. There is effective and selective use of evidence, with well-integrated short quotations that support analysis rather than retell the plot. Context is embedded thoughtfully into the discussion and these references are used to deepen interpretation, rather than being bolted on. The final paragraph offers a clear and insightful conclusion that draws together the ideas in a meaningful way. > **[exam-tip]** > - Focus on how different types of **powerlessness** are presented — mental, physical, social, racial and gender > - Show how **Lennie’s mental disability**, Candy’s **injury**, Crooks’ **race** and Curley’s wife’s **gender** each strip them of agency > - Embed **context** about the **Great Depression**, **racism** and **lack of support for the vulnerable** to explain why characters have so little control > - Reflect on how **George’s final decision** shows that even characters who seem in control are often **trapped by circumstance**

parts.problem_md:
Discuss Slim’s relationships with others on the ranch in Of Mice and Men.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In Of Mice and Men, Steinbeck presents Slim as a respected and thoughtful figure whose relationships with others on the ranch are characterised by authority, empathy and dignity. Slim’s interactions reveal his moral strength and show how he stands apart from the other men in both status and character.

Slim’s most notable relationship is with the other ranch workers, who clearly admire and respect him. Described as the “prince of the ranch” Slim carries himself with natural authority. When he speaks, “all talk stopped” and Steinbeck refers to the “gravity in his manner” and the “understanding beyond thought” that he possesses. Slim’s high status is also linked to his skill as a jerkline skinner, capable of handling “ten, sixteen, even twenty mules with a single line”. This practical ability, combined with his calm and fair nature, means that Slim’s opinions are treated almost like law: “his word was taken on any subject”. Candy, for example, looks to Slim in desperation, hoping he will stop Carlson from shooting his old dog. This shows how Slim’s opinion is valued above even that of the boss.

Slim’s relationship with George and Lennie is one of quiet understanding and respect. Unlike the boss or Curley, Slim does not question why the two men travel together. Instead, he accepts it as natural and even praises Lennie’s work: “He's a nice fella”. Slim’s kindness is particularly important for George, who opens up to him and shares the story of their escape from Weed. The fact that George confides in Slim suggests a rare moment of trust in a world where men are normally guarded. Slim is also sensitive to the depth of George and Lennie’s friendship, recognising that their companionship is something valuable and unusual on the ranch.

Slim also shows a respectful attitude towards characters who are otherwise marginalised, such as Crooks and Curley’s wife. He speaks to Crooks without using racist language and listens to him when he reports on Lennie’s behaviour, which contrasts with how the other men usually treat him. Similarly, Slim is the only man on the ranch who does not degrade Curley’s wife or objectify her. While he still joins the other men in going to the brothel, Steinbeck presents him as someone who sees people as individuals, not just as stereotypes.

Slim’s calm strength is also evident in his handling of conflict. When Curley accuses him of being with his wife, Slim immediately puts him in his place, causing Curley to back down: “Well, I didn’t mean nothing, Slim. I just ast you”. This moment shows how even the aggressive and confrontational Curley cannot intimidate Slim. Later, when Curley picks a fight with Lennie and has his hand crushed, it is Slim who takes control of the situation. He advises George to make Lennie let go and insists Curley lie about the cause of his injury: “I think you got your han' caught in a machine.” Slim’s ability to de-escalate conflict reinforces his position as a mediator and a man of fairness.

At the end of the novel, Slim plays a crucial role in helping George cope with the consequences of Lennie’s death. After George shoots Lennie to save him from Curley’s revenge, Slim is the only character who understands the difficult nature of George’s decision. He gently leads George away, saying “You hadda, George. I swear you had-da” and offers comfort: “Come on, George. Me an’ you’ll go in an’ get a drink”. This moment highlights Slim’s compassionate nature and the mutual respect between the two men.

Slim’s relationships are shaped by his detachment as well as his dignity. While he treats others with kindness and patience, he remains slightly distant, perhaps because he is more permanent and established than the other itinerant workers. His quiet distance sets him apart, but it also allows him to act as a fair judge of character, someone who sees beyond prejudice and pride. Steinbeck presents Slim as a thoughtful and sensitive man, in order to challenge the stereotypical perception of ranch hands.

In conclusion, Steinbeck presents Slim as a character who, while detached, maintains deeply respectful and understanding relationships with others. His kindness towards George, Lennie, Crooks and even Curley’s wife shows his moral integrity, while his authority over the other ranch hands highlights the respect he commands. parts.problem_md:
Explore the theme of dreams in Of Mice and Men.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Steinbeck presents the dream of owning land as a fragile source of hope that gives the powerless men of the ranch dignity and friendship, but which the harsh world of the Great Depression makes impossible to reach.

The central dream is George and Lennie’s plan to own a little place and “live off the fatta the lan’”. Steinbeck presents it almost as a ritual: Lennie begs George to repeat it, and the rehearsed words — Lennie chanting about how he will “tend the rabbits” — turn the dream into a comforting story they tell each other. Set during the Great Depression, when thousands of migrant workers drifted between ranches with no security, this dream of a home of their own is really a dream of stability and independence. Steinbeck uses it to show what these men long for: not wealth, but a place where nobody can sack them and where they belong.

The dream is also what makes George and Lennie different from other ranch hands. George reminds Lennie that, unlike the lonely men who work on ranches, “I got you to look after me, and you got me to look after you”. The balanced structure of the sentence mirrors the equal, two-way bond between them. The dream gives their friendship a purpose and lifts them above the loneliness Steinbeck shows everywhere else on the ranch. It briefly spreads hope to others too: when Candy overhears it, he offers his savings to join, and for a moment the dream seems almost within reach.

Steinbeck widens the theme by giving almost every character a broken dream. Curley’s wife clings to the memory that a man once promised to “put me in the movies” and insists she “coulda been in the movies”. Her dream of fame is presented as a fantasy built on a stranger’s empty promise, and her loneliness comes partly from the gap between that imagined life and her real one as the only woman on the ranch, trapped in an unhappy marriage. Through her, Steinbeck shows how limited women’s choices were in 1930s America and how dreams can become a way of escaping a life that offers nothing.

Steinbeck also uses Crooks to question whether any of these dreams can come true. Crooks has watched many men chase the same fantasy of land, and tells Lennie that “nobody gets no land” because “it’s just in their head”. As the only black man on the ranch, isolated by segregation and forced to live alone in the harness room, Crooks speaks from bitter experience. His blunt realism works as a warning to the reader: in a world this unequal, the dream is a comfort, not a plan. For a moment he is tempted to believe in it too, before Curley’s wife cruelly reminds him of his place.

The dream’s collapse is built into the novel’s structure. Steinbeck repeatedly has the men recite it just before things go wrong, so that hope and disaster are tied together. When Lennie accidentally kills Curley’s wife, the dream dies with her, and George’s decision to shoot Lennie himself is also the moment he gives up the future they planned. By ending the novel with George alone, Steinbeck suggests that in a society that values the strong over the weak, dreams of a better life are almost always crushed.

Through the dream of the farm, Steinbeck explores both the hope that keeps the powerless going and the harsh reality that defeats them. The dream gives the men dignity, friendship and a reason to carry on, but the world of the Great Depression makes it unreachable. Its destruction is Steinbeck’s quiet, angry comment on an America that promised opportunity to everyone but delivered it to almost no one.

> This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is an assured, wide-ranging response that explores the theme of dreams across the whole novel and integrates context throughout.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The answer keeps a tight focus on the theme of dreams and ranges across the novel — George and Lennie, Candy, Curley’s wife and Crooks — rather than narrating events. References are short and embedded (“the fatta the lan’”, “nobody gets no land”, “coulda been in the movies”), and methods are analysed rather than just named: the ritual repetition of the dream, the balanced sentence that mirrors George and Lennie’s bond, and the way Steinbeck recites the dream just before disaster strikes.
> 
> Context (AO3) is built into the argument — the Great Depression, migrant labour, women’s limited choices and segregation all support points rather than sitting in a separate paragraph. The response also moves beyond the literal, reading the broken dreams as a comment on the wider failure of the American Dream, which secures Level 5.
> 
> **Other arguments you could consider**
> 
> - A response could read the farm dream as Steinbeck’s critique of the American Dream itself, arguing the novel exposes that ideal as a myth for the poor.
> - A response could focus on Candy and his dog, exploring how his eagerness to join the dream reflects his fear of being discarded once he is too old to be useful.

> - Keep quotes short: “the fatta the lan’” or “nobody gets no land” is enough to anchor a point.
> - Weave context in — link the Great Depression and migrant work to why the men crave land, don’t bolt it on.
> - Explore Steinbeck’s structure: notice how the dream is recited just before things go wrong.
> - Go beyond the literal — the broken dreams comment on the wider failure of the American Dream.
> - Use Crooks and Curley’s wife to show how race and gender limit whose dreams can ever come true.
> - Plan your points so the essay covers the whole novel, ending with how and why the dream dies.
